alt: A lone reader with a book is set beside an audience watching two actors on stage. Four rows explain how this changes meaning: the audience sees silent characters, often knows more than a character, experiences timing controlled by the playwright and performers, and must infer motives without a narrator.
caption: A play’s meaning is made for an audience watching together in real time.

alt: Eight dramatic methods grouped by what the audience sees (stage directions, props and set, entrances and exits), hears (dialogue, soliloquy and aside, verse and prose) and knows (dramatic irony, structure). Each has what to look for and its typical effect.
caption: Every method is a way of shaping what the audience sees, hears or knows.

after: ## Worked example 1: reading a short scene as performance
alt: The guide’s invented kitchen scene with five details marked: the third plate as a prop, Daniel’s coat removed slowly but not hung up, the pause after “He won’t”, Mara straightening the fork instead of arguing, and her final line, which the audience hears as a refusal to give up.
caption: Props, stage directions and pauses carry the meaning, not just the words.

after: ## Worked example 2: building an essay on the whole play
alt: Five numbered stages for an essay on a parent and child relationship: an argument, the relationship’s first appearance on stage, a turning point or climax, the ending, and one precise context link. Below, each point pairs a quotation with a staging note.
caption: Move from first appearance to ending, and give every quotation a staging note.
